                                                        Abstract
     In lifelong learning, a learner faces a sequence of tasks with shared structure and aims to identify
     and leverage it to accelerate learning. We study the setting where such structure is captured by a
     common representation of data. Unlike multi-task learning or learning-to-learn, where tasks are
     available upfront to learn the representation, lifelong learning requires the learner to make use of
     its existing knowledge while continually gathering partial information in an online fashion. In
     this paper, we consider a generalized framework of lifelong representation learning. We propose
     a simple algorithm that uses multi-task empirical risk minimization as a subroutine and establish
     a sample complexity bound based on a new notion we introduce—the task-eluder dimension. Our
     result applies to a wide range of learning problems involving general function classes. As concrete
     examples, we instantiate our result on classification and regression tasks under noise.
     Keywords: Multi-task learning, representation learning, lifelong learning, online learning


1. Introduction
In many real-world settings, learning naturally involves a collection of related tasks (Caruana, 1997).
The ability to identify and leverage shared structure among tasks allows a learner to transfer knowl-
edge and accelerate learning. One common form of structure lies in a shared representation of data
such that simple functions operating on it can support effective and efficient learning across tasks.
For example, adapting linear classifiers over a pre-trained set of deep neural network features has
demonstrated state-of-the-art performance in computer vision (Donahue et al., 2014).
    The benefit of representation transfer is a central topic in the study of multi-task learning (MTL)
and learning to learn (LTL) (Baxter, 2000; Maurer et al., 2016; Tripuraneni et al., 2020; Aliakbar-
pour et al., 2024). In MTL, the learner is given a fixed set of tasks and aims to jointly learn a shared
representation and task-specific prediction layers. In LTL, also known as meta-learning, tasks are
drawn from an unknown distribution: the learner is first trained on a collection of tasks and then
evaluated on a new task sampled from the same distribution. In both cases, tasks are available up-
front, and LTL often relies on having enough diversity in seen tasks for the learner to fully identify
the representation before applying it in an unseen task (Tripuraneni et al., 2020; Du et al., 2021).
    However, learning may unfold over time, with tasks arriving in a sequence, as is the case in
how humans learn. On the one hand, the learner should be able to begin making use of the shared
structure before it is fully uncovered. On the other hand, the learner can always continually gather

    While MTL and LTL with a shared representation have been extensively studied, theoretical un-
derstanding of the lifelong/online regime remains relatively limited (see Section 6 for related work).
For binary classification under the noiseless, realizable assumption, Balcan et al. (2015) study life-
long learning of linear classifiers that lie in a low-dimensional linear subspace, while Pentina and
Urner (2016) analyze the setting where new tasks may be represented by weighted majority votes
over previously learned hypotheses from any ground class. More recently, Cao et al. (2022) con-
sider shared one-hidden-layer representations, again under the noiseless, realizable assumption. In
this work, our goal is to develop an algorithm and a theory for composite predictors over general
function classes in noisy but well-specified settings (Section 2). Our main contributions are:
1. We study a simple, provably efficient algorithm (Section 3) for lifelong representation learning
   with composite predictors ft ◦ h, where h ∈ H is a shared representation (e.g., a deep neural
   network) and ft ∈ F is a prediction layer specialized to task t (e.g., a linear function). Our
   algorithm is composed of two modular subroutines, few-shot property test and multi-task empir-
   ical risk minimization (ERM); see Figure 1. This design points toward a connection between the
   theory of lifelong learning and more practical algorithmic frameworks in real-world MTL.
2. We provide theoretical guarantees on the sample and space complexities of our algorithm (Sec-
   tion 4.3) based on a new complexity measure, the task-eluder dimension (Section 3.2). Together,
   our algorithm and complexity measure bridge lifelong learning and MTL: multi-task ERM serves
   as a mechanism for refining the learner’s representation in lifelong learning, and the task-eluder
   dimension bounds how many times it needs to be invoked. When the task-eluder dimension is
   small, the benefit of representation transfer in lifelong learning becomes more evident.
3. To demonstrate the applicability of our findings, we provide examples of how our result can be
   instantiated in noisy regression and classification tasks (Section 5), and we empirically validate
   our theoretical results on synthetic and semi-synthetic data (Section 7).

High-level overview. In our algorithm, the learner maintains a representation ĥ ∈ H, which is
initially learned from the first task. For each subsequent task, the learner performs a property test
to determine if there exists a prediction layer f ∈ F such that the predictor f ◦ ĥ has excess risk at

this restricted class has risk ϵ-close to that of the Bayes optimal predictor. This is done via few-shot
learning the prediction layer with ĥ frozen (see also Figure 1(a)), and requires a small number of
samples depending only on the complexity of F. We call this the few-shot property test.
     If the test succeeds, the learner simply retains ĥ and safely outputs the predictor (lines 8 to 9).

subset of tasks where few-shot property test previously failed—whose samples are stored in memory

representation for this subset of tasks. We note that only samples from tasks where the property test

3.2. The task-eluder dimension

a politician “elude” by answering questions without revealing their true position? Herein, we adapt

4. Theoretical guarantees
In this section, we first provide additional background and introduce a few technical tools for our
theoretical analysis (Section 4.1). We then introduce two benchmark algorithms (Section 4.2) before

6. Related work
Multi-task learning (Caruana, 1997) has been extensively studied in the literature; see (Zhang and
Yang, 2021) for a survey. Lifelong learning can be traced back to (Thrun and Mitchell, 1995). Since
then, it has seen applications in a wide range of domains, such as robotics (Lowrey et al., 2018),
computer vision (Rebuffi et al., 2017), and natural language processing (de Masson D’Autume et al.,
2019). See (Sodhani et al., 2022) for an introduction to various approaches to lifelong learning.
Techniques from MTL and LTL have also been extended to lifelong learning (Finn et al., 2019).
Much of the literature focuses on mitigating catastrophic forgetting (McCloskey and Cohen, 1989),
whereas our main objective is to provide a theoretical study on the benefit of representation transfer.
    In particular, our work builds upon a line of research that studies sample complexity guaran-
tees of MTL and LTL where tasks share a common representation. Baxter (2000) study a general
framework for inductive bias learning and establish guarantees based on covering numbers of the
hypothesis space family. Maurer et al. (2016) use Gaussian complexities with a chain rule (Maurer,
2016) to derive data-dependent bounds. Tripuraneni et al. (2020) introduce a notion of task diver-
sity which characterizes when transfer learning of representations can be achieved in LTL. Xu and
Tewari (2021) study the setting where source and target tasks may use different classes of prediction

These papers all consider the composite model f ◦ h that we study in this work.
     MTL and LTL with shared linear representations have been studied (Tripuraneni et al., 2021;
Du et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2022; Aliakbarpour et al., 2024). PAC-Bayesian bounds for LTL, with
instantiations for parameter transfer and linear representation transfer, are developed by Pentina
and Lampert (2014). Pentina and Ben-David (2015) study MTL and LTL of kernels, and Pentina
and Ben-David (2018) approach MTL using probabilistic Lipschitzness as a quality measure of
kernels.Sequential and parallel representation transfer have also been explored for linear bandits
and RL (Hu et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2021; Qin et al., 2022; Duong et al., 2024).
     Our work is most directly related to (Balcan et al., 2015; Pentina and Urner, 2016; Cao et al.,
2022). These papers focus on lifelong learning for binary classification in the noiseless, realizable
setting. Balcan et al. (2015) study low-dimensional linear representations: each task’s predictor
is a linear combination of k shared basis vectors. Pentina and Urner (2016) use weighted ma-
jority votes over a growing set of previously learned base hypotheses from a ground class. Cao
et al. (2022) consider representations in the form of one hidden layer feature maps (a linear map
followed by a nonlinear activation). We note that the guarantee for nonlinear representations in
(Cao et al., 2022) relies on an assumption (Assumption 1 therein) that for two maps u and v,
d(u, v) ≲ PrPX (sign(u(x)) ̸= sign(v(x))) ≲ d(u, v), where d(·, ·) denotes the angle. While this
is true for linear maps when PX is isotropic, log-concave, the first inequality may not hold in general
for one-hidden-layer neural networks under the same assumption5 . Algorithmically, these papers
can be viewed as dynamically expanding their representation, with (Cao et al., 2022) additionally
performing refinement. In contrast, we work with composite predictors f ◦ h that predict through a
fixed H, and we use multi-task ERM to relearn our representation when it becomes insufficient.
     Li et al. (2022b) propose an architecture-based algorithm for continual representation learning.
They provide sample complexity bounds under an assumption of sequential task diversity: earlier
tasks are diverse enough to ensure small representational mismatch for new tasks. Similar assump-
tions have been made in (Tripuraneni et al., 2020) for LTL and (Qin et al., 2022) for sequential
transfer in linear bandits. In contrast, we consider an online setting where the task sequence may be
chosen by an adversary, and the learner needs to carefully manage when to request more data.
     Alquier et al. (2017) study lifelong representation learning in an online-within-online setting:
tasks arrive sequentially, and within each task, data points are also revealed sequentially with the
learner predicting each instance. They also consider a batch-within-online setting, where data from
each task is made available all at once. Alquier et al. (2017) study and establish compound regret
bounds of the learner. In contrast, we allow the learner to request samples over multiple rounds, and
require that, with high probability, it outputs for every task a predictor with excess risk at most ϵ.

Understanding how to ensure that such conditions hold, both in terms of the number of samples
needed and algorithmic techniques, would be an interesting direction for future study, with poten-
tial connections to collaborative PAC learning (Blum et al., 2017). At the same time, it is important
to also understand whether such definitions admit meaningful bounds on their induced notions of
task-eluder dimension for natural function classes.
     Beyond this, several other open questions remain. In this work, we assumed a well-specified
model (Assumpton 1). While this relaxes the noiseless, realizable assumption studied in prior work,
it remains to be seen if it can be further weakened. Other future directions include studying whether
the learner can infer noise levels from other tasks under additional structural assumptions, and
bounding the task-eluder dimension for more general function classes.

D.1. Implementation details
All implementations were developed in PyTorch. Most experiments were conducted on machines
equipped with NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPUs.
Synthetic linear experiments. For data generation, in each trial, B ∗ was obtained from the QR
decomposition of a random d × k matrix with standard normal entries, and wt∗ ’s were drawn from
the uniform distribution over the origin-centered sphere with radius β. For both multi-task ERM
and few-shot property tests, we used batch gradient descent with the Adam optimizer (Kingma,
2014) (learning rate 10−3 ), for a maximum of 104 epochs with early stopping after 20 epochs
without improvement. The Bayes-optimal risks were estimated via Monte-Carlo simulations from
106 samples.
MNIST experiments. Both multi-task ERM and few-shot property tests used batch gradient de-
scent with the Adam optimizer (learning rate 10−3 ), for up to 2000 epochs. For multi-task ERM,
early stopping was applied after 10 epochs without improvement.
CIFAR-10 experiments. We consider representations given by a modified ResNet-18 architec-
ture (He et al., 2016). The initial convolutional layer is replaced by a 3 × 3 kernel with stride 1,
with the remaining convolutional blocks kept unchanged. After the convolutional blocks, we apply
global average pooling, followed by a fully-connected linear layer, batch normalization, and ReLU
activation. The resulting representation is of dimension k = 256. All representation networks were
trained from scratch without any pretrained weights.
    For multi-task ERM, we used mini-batch stochastic gradient descent with the Adam optimizer
(learning rate 10−3 ), a batch size of 256, and trained for up to 300 epochs with early stopping after
20 epochs without improvement. For few-shot property tests, we used batch gradient descent with
the Adam optimizer (learning rate 10−2 ) for a maximum of 200 epochs.
